title: Ice Cream 1.5L

drivers.name: Price increase (2.3%)
drivers.evidence: One prior week with same price increase saw sales 43% below baseline; noise-adjusted effect suggests 25% lift reduction. No other similar events. Shrink toward 1.0 due to low evidence count.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 41.7. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increased by 2.3% to $6.56. Recent data shows a dip to 24 units in the week after a price increase (2026-09-28), which was 43% below baseline. Past promotions (median lift x1.57, noise-adjusted x1.25) are not active. The post-promotion effect is a known demand drop (x0.72, noise-adjusted x0.82), but no promotion occurred recently. The price rise is a clear demand reducer. Evidence from the recent price increase week supports a downside effect. The classical model suggests no uplift, consistent with no known drivers. The price effect is supported by a single past data point with a meaningful drop. Shrink the effect toward 1.0 due to low evidence count. No seasonal or trend shifts override this. The baseline already captures seasonal trends.

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 6.56 (+2.3% vs regular price 6.41)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 41.7 | 5%-95%: 17.1 - 65.0 | 10%-90%: 23.7 - 61.7

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-35% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
